theory.title: Perception, interpretation and cognitive bias
theory.explanation: Examine how attention, prior assumptions and cognitive shortcuts shape interpretation; distinguish observation from inference and test conclusions against counter-evidence.
theory.tip: Use precise terms, seek disconfirming evidence and avoid conclusions that exceed the available data. Generated pronunciation audio remains pending review.

reading.english:
How Perception Shapes Judgement

We rarely encounter information without interpretation. Attention selects some details and leaves others in the background; prior expectations then influence the meaning we assign to what remains. Cognitive biases are not evidence that people are irrational in every respect. They are recurring shortcuts that can be useful under pressure but unreliable when decisions require careful comparison.

Confirmation bias encourages us to notice evidence that supports an existing view. The availability heuristic makes vivid or recent examples seem more common than they are. Anchoring can give an initial figure disproportionate influence, even when better information later becomes available. Framing also matters: the same outcome may appear attractive or alarming depending on how it is presented.

Awareness alone does not eliminate these effects. A more disciplined approach involves asking what evidence would change our minds, checking how a sample was selected and considering plausible alternatives. In public debate, this means distinguishing observation from interpretation and resisting conclusions that exceed the evidence. Sound judgement is not the absence of bias, but the willingness to examine and correct it.
reading.spanish: Cómo la percepción condiciona el juicio. El texto examina la atención selectiva, los sesgos cognitivos y estrategias para evaluar pruebas y alternativas.
